name: Why gold: the convergent monetary properties
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: Why every literate civilization independently converged on gold as money. T1: gold appears as money in Egypt (Nubian mines, 4000 BC onward), Rome (aureus, denarius silver), China (gold ingots under the Han), the Andes (Inca ceremonial gold), and West Africa (Mansa Musa's Mali empire) -- with NO contact between these civilizations at the time of adoption. T2: the classical list of MONETARY PROPERTIES a good must have: DURABILITY (does not rot or rust), PORTABILITY (high value per unit weight), DIVISIBILITY (can be split without loss of value), FUNGIBILITY (one unit interchangeable with another), SCARCITY (cannot be made at will), RECOGNIZABILITY (traders can verify it on sight). Gold scores highest on all six. T3: the PROPERTY-BY-PROPERTY comparison. Iron rusts (durability fails); cattle are hard to carry (portability fails); diamonds cannot be divided without loss (divisibility fails); art is not fungible (each piece unique); seashells and clay tokens can be gathered or fired at will (scarcity fails); pyrite looks like gold but has half the density (recognizability -- traders learn the bite test and the weight test). T4: SCARCITY-IN-DEPTH -- Saifedean Ammous's STOCK-TO-FLOW ratio in The Bitcoin Standard (2018): gold has the highest stock-to-flow of any physical commodity, roughly 60 (60 years of current production to equal existing above-ground stock), because all the gold ever mined is still around and annual production adds only ~1.5%. Silver's stock-to-flow is ~22, copper's is <1. T5: the RECOGNITION MOVE the ladder teaches -- CONVERGENT SELECTION across isolated civilizations is EVIDENCE that gold's monetary role is not cultural accident but a physical-property result. Any candidate for money must beat gold on at least one property WITHOUT losing others -- which is the exact test Bitcoin was engineered to pass (unlimited divisibility, effortless portability by wire, verifiable scarcity capped at 21M, cryptographic recognizability).
source: PRIMARY: Saifedean Ammous, The Bitcoin Standard (2018) chapters 1-2 (monetary properties and stock-to-flow). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Gold as an investment', 'Monetary metal', 'Stock-to-flow model' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- the six classical monetary properties, gold's convergent independent adoption across civilizations, stock-to-flow figures. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the ~60 stock-to-flow figure for gold; the ~1.5% annual mine production rate; Mansa Musa's 1324 hajj as canonical convergent-adoption example.
framing_note: The framework rung that lets a kid answer 'why gold?' by REASONING from physical properties, not memorizing 'gold is valuable.' Bastiat-pattern payoff: T3 (the SEEN candidate money -- seashells -- fails the UNSEEN scarcity test because anyone can gather more). T5 sets up the whole Bitcoin case that follows: gold's engineering wins get replicated and improved by cryptographic engineering. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem list the six properties and ask 'why is gold money?' -- give a specific alternative (iron, cattle, seashells, diamonds) and ask which property IT fails on. DISTRACTOR MINE: other real proposed monies (silver, copper, cowries, wampum, tally sticks, salt -- Roman soldiers' salarium), other named theorists (Menger on saleability, Mises on the regression theorem, Rothbard on 100% reserve gold). TEACH-BEFORE-TEST anchor for Ammous as a named figure -- his Bitcoin Standard book is referenced repeatedly later; grade-10 register throughout.
history_overlap: GEOGRAPHY owns the mining locations (Nubian gold country, Andean mountains, Potosi mountain of silver) -- economics owns WHY gold specifically won as money.

name: Rai stones of Yap: the sunken money still recognized
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The Pacific island monetary system Milton Friedman used to explain the Federal Reserve. T1: on YAP ISLAND in Micronesia, for centuries, the money was RAI STONES -- massive round limestone discs, some over 12 feet across and weighing tons, quarried on the island of PALAU 250 miles away and transported by outrigger canoe. T2: the stones were TOO HEAVY TO MOVE around the island once installed. Ownership transferred by public COMMUNITY MEMORY -- villagers agreed 'that stone is now Anua's, not Fatumak's' and the physical stone stayed where it was. T3: the famous SUNKEN STONE. A canoe crew was bringing a particularly large rai back from Palau when a storm came up and the stone slipped into the sea, sinking hundreds of feet down. The crew returned and testified to its exact size and quality. The islanders AGREED it was still valuable, still ownable, still transferable -- even though no living person would ever see it again. T4: Milton FRIEDMAN wrote about this in a 1991 essay 'The Island of Stone Money' (later collected in Money Mischief 1992). His point: Yap's ledger-of-ownership-without-physical-transfer is EXACTLY what the Federal Reserve does with the US gold at Fort Knox -- the gold rarely moves; the CLAIMS to it move. And what the Bank of France did in 1932-33, when it wanted to convert dollar-claims to gold: the Federal Reserve Bank of New York simply moved gold bars from one labeled drawer in its vault to another. The bars did not leave the building. Their national ownership changed anyway. T5: the DEEP LESSON Friedman drew and cypherpunks later drew: MONEY IS A LEDGER. The physical medium is a container for social agreement about who owns what. Once you see this, the leap to a purely digital ledger enforced by cryptography rather than community memory -- Bitcoin's Nakamoto ledger -- is a natural extension, not a break from monetary tradition.
source: PRIMARY: Milton Friedman, 'The Island of Stone Money' (Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, February 1991), reprinted in Money Mischief: Episodes in Monetary History (1992). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Rai stones' and 'Yap' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- rai as limestone discs quarried on Palau, transported by canoe, ownership tracked by community memory, the sunken-stone anecdote (originally recorded by anthropologist William Henry Furness III in his 1910 book The Island of Stone Money), Friedman's 1991 essay drawing the Fort Knox and Bank of France 1932-33 parallels. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the Furness 1910 primary source; the specific Bank of France 1932-33 episode Friedman cites.
framing_note: A story-first rung that a kid will actually remember at dinner and that carries a load-bearing reasoning payoff. Bastiat-pattern payoff: T3 (the SEEN money -- the giant stone -- is at the bottom of the sea, but the UNSEEN LEDGER of ownership continues to function; the ledger IS the money). T4/T5 build the bridge from stone-age money to Bitcoin: the community memory is the ancestor of the blockchain. TEACH-BEFORE-TEST: Friedman gets his foundational anchor here (referenced in Fed pillar, Great Depression rung, and inflation-monetary-phenomenon rungs). SYMMETRIC-VOICE: told as anthropology, not as 'primitive money' -- the Yap system worked for centuries. DISTRACTOR MINE: other unusual real historical monies (cowrie shells across the Indian Ocean and West African trade, wampum in colonial New England, tally sticks in medieval England, salt bricks in the Sahara).

name: The Roman denarius debasement (64 AD - 274 AD)
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The two-century slow-motion collapse of the Roman silver coinage -- the historical template for every debasement since. T1: the DENARIUS was Rome's standard silver coin. Under AUGUSTUS (27 BC - 14 AD) it was roughly 98% silver, and stayed near that purity for nearly a century. T2: the first major debasement came under NERO in 64 AD -- Nero cut the silver content to about 93% and reduced the weight, using the recovered silver to pay for imperial spending and the rebuilding of Rome after the Great Fire. T3: over the next 200 years successive emperors quietly reduced the silver content each time they needed to pay soldiers or fund campaigns. By the reign of GALLIENUS in the 260s AD, the 'silver' denarius was about 5% silver -- essentially a bronze coin with a thin silver wash that flaked off in circulation. T4: DIOCLETIAN'S EDICT ON MAXIMUM PRICES in 301 AD -- Diocletian, seeing prices spiral, decreed maximum legal prices for over 1,000 goods and services, with the DEATH PENALTY for merchants who charged more. The result was NOT stable prices -- merchants simply withdrew their goods from public sale, black markets sprang up, and shortages appeared. Diocletian's own inscriptions (found across the empire) record the failure. T5: the DEEP MOVE the ladder teaches -- debasement is a HIDDEN TAX (Cantillon effect: the emperor who spends the newly-diluted coin first gets full value; the citizens receiving it later find it buys less). Diocletian's failure teaches that PRICE CONTROLS on top of debasement produce SHORTAGES not stability, because the underlying cause -- the debased currency -- is untouched. The Roman pattern will recur exactly: Weimar wage controls, Nixon's 1971 wage/price freeze, Venezuela's Maduro-era price ceilings, all with the same shortage-and-black-market result.
source: PRIMARY: Diocletian's Edict on Maximum Prices (301 AD, preserved in ~40 inscription fragments across the empire, most complete at Aphrodisias); Kenneth Harl, Coinage in the Roman Economy 300 BC to 700 AD (1996) for silver-content figures. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Roman currency', 'Denarius', 'Debasement', 'Edict on Maximum Prices' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- Augustus's 98% silver denarius, Nero's 64 AD debasement, the century-by-century decline to ~5% by Gallienus, Diocletian's 301 AD edict with death penalty and merchant withdrawal from public sale. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: exact silver-content percentages by emperor (Harl's figures are the scholarly standard); the number of goods listed in the Edict (~1,200 in the Aphrodisias copy).
framing_note: The bank's first HISTORICAL DEBASEMENT ladder -- kid learns the pattern once here and recognizes it in every later rung. Bastiat-pattern payoff: T4 (the SEEN price cap looks like it stops inflation; the UNSEEN merchant withdrawal empties the shops). T5 makes the recognition move explicit: debasement is a hidden tax on the poor and on savers. ANTI-RESTATEMENT: never let the stem say 'inflation' or 'debasement' and ask what happened -- describe the SPECIFIC EMPEROR, the SILVER CONTENT DROP, the EDICT with its death penalty, and let the answer NAME the emperor or the specific mechanism. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the answer names the Cantillon MOVE (early spenders capture value; savers absorb the loss), not 'Rome was bad.' DISTRACTOR MINE: other real Roman economic events (Sulla's proscriptions, Julius Caesar's debt-jubilee laws, Constantine's 312 AD solidus reform which was an OPPOSITE move -- restoring gold coinage); other real historical price-control failures (Hammurabi's wage schedule; Colbert's French price fixing; British WWI food controls).
history_overlap: HISTORY owns Diocletian as emperor and the Tetrarchy political reforms -- economics owns the MONETARY debasement and the PRICE-CONTROL FAILURE as reasoning cases.

name: Jiaozi and Kublai Khan: the first paper money bubbles
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The Chinese invention of paper money -- and its immediate hyperinflation, twice. T1: in Sichuan province during the 11th-century SONG DYNASTY, merchants began issuing paper receipts called JIAOZI backed by deposits of iron coins (which were bulky and heavy for large transactions). The Song government took over the issuance around 1023 AD, making jiaozi the world's first widely-circulated government paper money. T2: the discipline held for about 40 years. But by the late Song, the government was issuing jiaozi faster than any specie backing could support, using the printing to fund military campaigns against the Jin and later the Mongols. By the early 13th century the jiaozi had lost most of its value -- within ~200 years of its birth, the first fiat currency had hyperinflated. T3: the MONGOLS conquered Song China and KUBLAI KHAN (reigned 1260-1294) issued his own paper currency, the CHAO. Unlike Song paper, the chao had no metal backing at all -- it was declared legal tender by imperial decree. Kublai enforced acceptance under threat of severe punishment; according to Marco Polo's Travels, refusing the paper was PUNISHABLE BY DEATH. T4: Marco POLO'S astonishment at the system -- he devotes a whole chapter of his Travels (c. 1298) to describing how the Great Khan makes 'money out of the bark of trees' (mulberry-bark paper), how each note is stamped with vermilion by imperial officials, and how it circulates 'as if it were pure gold or silver.' Polo calls it a kind of ALCHEMY -- the Khan's magic that turns bark into wealth. T5: the pattern the ladder teaches. The chao held its value while Kublai lived and the empire projected force. Within a generation of his death the successor Yuan emperors printed at will to fund crises; by the 1350s the chao was worthless and the Yuan dynasty was collapsing. Two Chinese paper-money experiments; two hyperinflations; the pattern the Austrians say is inescapable: paper money without discipline becomes political money, and political money always dies.
source: PRIMARY: Marco Polo, Il Milione (The Travels, c. 1298), Book II, chapter on the Great Khan's money. CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Jiaozi (currency)', 'Chao (currency)', 'Song dynasty', 'History of Chinese currency', 'Marco Polo' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- jiaozi as Song-era world-first paper money (Sichuan merchants ~1000 AD, government takeover 1023), hyperinflation within 200 years; Kublai Khan's chao as unbacked fiat, mulberry-bark paper, Marco Polo's astonished account, Yuan-dynasty collapse tied to chao hyperinflation. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the 1023 government-takeover date; the death-penalty detail (attribute EXPLICITLY to Marco Polo's account rather than as neutral fact -- Polo's numbers are sometimes disputed); the mulberry-bark material.
framing_note: The ladder that lets a kid say 'wait, paper money is NINE HUNDRED YEARS OLD and it hyperinflated the FIRST TWO TIMES anyone tried it?' Bastiat-pattern payoff: T4 (the SEEN wonder of bark-becoming-wealth is what dazzled Polo; the UNSEEN political dynamic -- printing to fund war -- kills every such experiment within a generation or two). ACCURACY RAIL: the death-penalty-for-refusing-paper detail comes from POLO'S account; attribute it to him rather than as bare fact ('according to Marco Polo, the Khan enforced acceptance under penalty of death'). SCENE-LED never definition-shell: never 'what is fiat currency?' -- always the specific bark-paper stamped in vermilion. DISTRACTOR MINE: other early currency innovations (Lydian electrum coins ~600 BC; the Athenian owl tetradrachm; Byzantine solidus; medieval European jettons); other Marco Polo details (the Silk Road, Kublai's summer palace at Shangdu -- Coleridge's Xanadu). Do NOT let a rung claim Polo INVENTED paper money -- he witnessed and described it.
history_overlap: HISTORY owns the Song and Yuan dynasties as political entities; GEOGRAPHY owns China and the Silk Road as places -- economics owns the MONETARY EXPERIMENTS specifically.

name: Potosi silver and the Price Revolution (1545-1650)
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The first global monetary shock, and the first serious analysis of it. T1: in 1545, in the highlands of what is now Bolivia, a native Andean discovered a mountain of silver at POTOSI. The Spanish crown quickly claimed it. Within a generation Potosi was the largest city in the Americas, producing more silver than all of Europe combined -- roughly 60% of world silver output between 1550 and 1650. T2: the silver flowed east on the Spanish TREASURE FLEETS (Flota de Indias), across the Atlantic to Seville, and from Seville out into European commerce. Prices in Spain and across western Europe rose STEADILY for over a century -- historians estimate a roughly 500% rise in general price level from 1500 to 1650 across the continent (the PRICE REVOLUTION). T3: the QUANTITY-THEORY-OF-MONEY insight in embryonic form. Even mercantilist writers who thought hoarding gold made a nation rich began to notice that Spain, which had the MOST bullion, was becoming POORER (its industry hollowed out, its farmers priced out of European markets, its debt to Genoese bankers spiraling). More silver in circulation raised prices; higher prices made Spanish exports uncompetitive. T4: MARTIN DE AZPILCUETA, a Spanish theologian at the SALAMANCA SCHOOL, wrote in his 1556 Commentary on the Resolution of Money the first clear statement in Europe of what became the quantity theory: 'money is worth more where and when it is scarce than where and when it is abundant.' Azpilcueta and his fellow Salamancans (Luis de Molina, Domingo de Soto) were reasoning about prices, interest, and money 200 years before Adam Smith. T5: the RECOGNITION MOVE the ladder teaches. What looked like SEEN NATIONAL WEALTH (galleons of silver arriving in Seville) was actually UNSEEN NATIONAL IMPOVERISHMENT (Spanish industry destroyed, savers debased, the crown chronically bankrupt despite the flood of bullion). The Salamanca insight -- that more money means higher prices, not more real wealth -- is the exact reasoning that later Austrians apply to central-bank money printing.
source: PRIMARY: Martin de Azpilcueta, Comentario resolutorio de cambios (1556, Coimbra). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Potosi', 'Price revolution', 'School of Salamanca', 'Martin de Azpilcueta', 'Spanish treasure fleet' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- 1545 Potosi discovery, ~60% of world silver output 1550-1650, ~500% European price rise, Salamanca school as proto-Austrians, Azpilcueta 1556 quantity-of-money insight, Spain's paradoxical impoverishment. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the 500% price-rise figure (specifically Hamilton 1934 American Treasure and the Price Revolution in Spain is the seminal source); the 1545 Potosi discovery date; Azpilcueta 1556 text.
framing_note: A ladder that quietly does TWO jobs -- it teaches the quantity theory in its historical birth, and it establishes the SALAMANCA SCHOOL as a real 16th-century predecessor to the Austrians (correcting the standard textbook claim that economics began with Adam Smith 1776). Bastiat-pattern payoff: T5 (SEEN silver arriving in Seville looks like wealth; UNSEEN industry-hollowing and savings-debasement is the actual result). ACCURACY RAIL: the Potosi discovery date is 1545; the mountain the Spanish worked was Cerro Rico ('rich mountain') towering over the town. RECOGNITION-NOT-VERDICT: the answer names the MOVE (money-supply expansion raises prices without raising real wealth), not 'Spain deserved it.' DISTRACTOR MINE: other named Salamancans (Luis de Molina on just price, Francisco de Vitoria on natural law, Domingo de Soto on labor value), other early monetary theorists (Copernicus's 1526 Monetae cudendae ratio, Jean Bodin 1568 on the same price-revolution), other Spanish silver-fleet events (the 1628 Piet Heyn capture at Matanzas Bay). Do NOT confuse Potosi (Bolivia) with Pachuca or Zacatecas (Mexican silver mines that produced the New Spain reales).

name: John Law and the Mississippi Bubble (1716-1720)
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The first modern paper-money bubble, and the man who inflated it. T1: JOHN LAW, a Scottish gambler and monetary theorist, arrived in France in 1715 after fleeing a duel-killing in London. France was on the edge of bankruptcy from Louis XIV's wars, and the regent for the child-king Louis XV -- the DUKE OF ORLEANS -- listened to Law's plan. T2: in 1716 Law founded the BANQUE GENERALE, a private note-issuing bank; in 1718 it became the BANQUE ROYALE, effectively France's central bank, with the state guaranteeing its notes. In 1717 Law also founded the COMPAGNIE DU MISSISSIPPI (the Mississippi Company), which held the trade monopoly for France's Louisiana colony. T3: Law's SCHEME. The bank issued paper money; the Mississippi Company issued shares; the paper money could be used to buy shares; the shares' rising price made people demand more paper money; the bank printed more; the shares rose more. Between 1719 and 1720, Mississippi Company shares rose from about 500 livres to over 10,000 livres -- a 20-fold gain in months. Ordinary Parisians (the word MILLIONAIRE was coined in this bubble) grew rich on paper. T4: the COLLAPSE. In early 1720 some large holders began cashing in shares for the paper money and demanding gold in exchange. The bank could not honor the redemptions. Law tried to ban private gold ownership (February 1720) -- it failed. He devalued the currency, then re-valued it, then decreed multiple contradictory laws in weeks. By late 1720 the shares were worthless, the paper money was worthless, and Law fled France in disgrace, dying poor in Venice in 1729. T5: the LESSONS the ladder teaches -- exactly the pattern every fiat inflation since has followed. SEEN: newly rich shareholders, apparent boom, roads paved, palaces built. UNSEEN: real capital allocated to the fantasy Louisiana venture instead of productive uses; savers destroyed when the paper collapsed; French monetary confidence damaged for a full generation (France resisted paper money for the next 70 years -- until the Assignat, which was the SECOND time the same country tried it, with the same result). Law's scheme is the first case where the Austrian ABCT pattern is visible in modern form: paper-money expansion drove asset-price boom, malinvestment concentrated in one project, redemption run collapsed the whole edifice.
source: PRIMARY: John Law, Money and Trade Considered (1705); Antoin Murphy, John Law: Economic Theorist and Policy-Maker (1997). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'John Law (economist)', 'Mississippi Company', 'Banque Royale', 'Mississippi Bubble' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- 1716 Banque Generale, 1718 Banque Royale, 1717 Mississippi Company, share price rise from ~500 to ~10,000 livres 1719-20, the 'millionaire' coinage, the 1720 collapse, Law's flight to Venice and 1729 death. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the specific share-price peak figure; the 1715 arrival date; the Duke of Orleans as regent (not Louis XV personally, who was 5 years old); the 1729 death date in Venice.
framing_note: The ladder that makes a kid see that BUBBLES ARE NOT NEW. Bastiat-pattern payoff: T5 (SEEN Paris rich with new millionaires; UNSEEN capital destroyed and generation-long distrust of paper money). SCENE-LED: never 'what is a bubble?' -- always the specific Paris scene, the specific share price, the specific Louisiana project. name: The Continental (1775-1781): 'not worth a Continental'
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The American Revolution's paper money and the folk phrase it left behind. T1: when the Continental Congress voted for war in 1775, it had no power to tax -- only the states did. To pay for soldiers, supplies, and gunpowder, Congress AUTHORIZED PAPER MONEY called CONTINENTAL CURRENCY (or simply CONTINENTALS), beginning with $2 million in June 1775. T2: the states also printed their own paper money. Over the six years of the war, the Continental Congress authorized issue after issue -- roughly $241 MILLION in Continentals were printed, at a time when total specie (gold and silver coin) circulating in the colonies was estimated at only about $6 million. T3: the RESULT. By early 1781 a Continental dollar was worth about one-fortieth of a silver dollar; by the summer of 1781 it was worth about one-hundredth; by the end of the year it was effectively worthless. Barbers papered their shops with Continentals as decoration. The FOLK PHRASE 'not worth a Continental' entered American English and remained current for a century. T4: the QUIET CATASTROPHE the phrase hides. Soldiers were paid in Continentals -- their families' savings evaporated. Farmers who accepted Continentals in payment for grain became poor; those who insisted on gold were called price-gougers. Congress tried WAGE AND PRICE CONTROLS in 1777 and 1778 -- they failed. Some states tried LEGAL-TENDER LAWS threatening prison for refusing Continentals -- they were widely evaded. T5: the CONSTITUTIONAL LESSON the founders drew. When the US Constitution was drafted in 1787, the delegates -- Madison and Hamilton in particular -- specifically FORBADE the states from issuing 'bills of credit' (paper money) and specifically LIMITED Congress's monetary powers to 'coin Money, regulate the value thereof' (Article I Section 8). The famous phrase 'not worth a Continental' was a living memory for every man in the Philadelphia convention; the founders' hard-money bias was an EMPIRICAL LESSON drawn from the recent catastrophic experiment they had lived through.

CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Continental currency', 'Not worth a Continental', 'History of United States currency' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- ~$241M total Continental issue, ~$6M specie circulation, collapse to 1:100 by end of 1781, the folk phrase, the Constitutional response in 1787. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the specific $241M total figure (Grubb 2008 is the definitive scholarly source); the June 1775 first-issue date; the Article I Section 10 text banning state bills of credit.

Bastiat-pattern payoff: T4 (SEEN government paying soldiers; UNSEEN soldiers' families ruined when the paper collapsed; SEEN wage/price controls stabilizing markets; UNSEEN goods withdrawn from public sale). name: The Assignat (1789-1796): French Revolution's paper money
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The paper money that funded the Terror -- and the definitive 1912 account of it. T1: in November 1789 the revolutionary National Assembly, needing money and having none, seized the lands of the CATHOLIC CHURCH in France (about 15% of French land) and used them as collateral for a new paper currency: the ASSIGNAT. Each note was legally a claim on future land sales. T2: the first issue was 400 million livres, and the assembly promised solemnly that it would be the ONLY issue. Within months a second issue followed, then a third. By 1795 total assignats in circulation exceeded 40 BILLION livres -- 100 times the original 'only' issue. T3: the COLLAPSE. Prices doubled and doubled again. Peasants refused assignats and demanded gold; the government responded with laws forbidding preference for coin, penalties for refusing paper, and eventually the death penalty for currency speculators. By 1796 an assignat was worth about 1/1000 of its face value; the government withdrew the currency and tried again with the MANDATS TERRITORIAUX -- which collapsed even faster. T4: the HISTORICAL PARALLELS that make this rung load-bearing. The Assignat is the SECOND time France tried paper money (Law's 1720 Banque Royale was the first). Same country, same 76-year gap, SAME COMPLETE COLLAPSE. Every mechanism the Revolution used (legal tender coercion, price controls, death penalty for gold hoarders) was tried by the Continental Congress a decade earlier and would be tried by Weimar Germany a century later. T5: ANDREW DICKSON WHITE'S FIAT MONEY INFLATION IN FRANCE (1912). White (co-founder and first president of Cornell University) wrote a slim book documenting the Assignat episode as a warning to his own era's paper-money advocates. His conclusion, still quoted by Austrian economists: 'The one thing that no government could do -- neither Assembly, nor Convention, nor Directory -- was to make paper money worth as much as gold when there was more paper than the land could redeem.' The book has been in print continuously since 1912 and is the standard Austrian-libertarian reference for the Assignat collapse.
source: PRIMARY: Andrew Dickson White, Fiat Money Inflation in France (1912, Cobden Club). CONSULTED: Grokipedia 'Assignat', 'French Revolution', 'Andrew Dickson White', 'Mandat territorial' (browser, 2026-09-05) -- November 1789 first issue backed by church-lands, 400M livre original limit vs 40B by 1795, price controls and death penalty for gold hoarding, 1796 assignat withdrawal, mandat territorial replacement collapse, White's 1912 book as canonical Austrian reference. CORROBORATE AT BUILD: the November 1789 first-issue date; the 40 billion livre 1795 figure; White's exact 1912 publication.
framing_note: The ladder that shows the SAME COUNTRY hyperinflated paper money TWICE within a century. name: The Classical Gold Standard (1815-1914)
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The century of sound money -- and the last time the West lived under it. T1: in 1821 BRITAIN formally adopted the GOLD STANDARD -- committing that the Bank of England would redeem paper pound notes for gold at a FIXED PRICE (about 4.86 pounds per troy ounce, which had been the informal rate since 1717). This became the model for the whole industrial world. T2: between 1870 and 1900 the major industrial powers joined -- Germany 1871 (using French war reparations from the Franco-Prussian War to fund the transition), the United States 1873 formally and 1900 with the Gold Standard Act, France and the Latin Monetary Union effectively, Japan 1897, Russia 1897. By 1900, nearly the entire industrial world traded on a shared gold basis. T3: what a SHARED GOLD STANDARD meant in practice. Exchange rates between currencies were FIXED (a pound was always ~4.86 dollars) because both were fixed to gold. International capital moved freely across borders without exchange-rate risk. A worker in London could remit wages to his family in Naples and the money kept its value. Prices in Britain from 1821 to 1914 were REMARKABLY STABLE -- the price level in 1914 was roughly the same as in 1821, with fluctuations but no long-term trend. T4: the BELLE EPOQUE (1871-1914) as the era's fruit. Cross-border investment in railways, telegraphs, canals, industry hit historical highs; European emigration to the Americas and Australia was funded by private savings that held their value; the middle class expanded dramatically; life expectancy rose; a working-class family in 1913 was much better fed than in 1870. Ludwig von Mises later wrote that the gold standard was 'the most important instrument of the constitution of freedom.' T5: the DEEP MOVE the ladder teaches. Under gold, GOVERNMENTS CANNOT FUND WAR BY INFLATION -- they must tax, borrow, or lose. The classical gold standard imposed a HARD BUDGET CONSTRAINT on the state. This is exactly why it did not survive WW1: belligerents in August 1914 suspended gold convertibility within days, so they could print money to fund the war. The century of stable prices ended not because the gold standard failed but because states wanted to fight a war that gold-discipline would have made unaffordable.

name: Gresham's Law: bad money drives out good
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The 500-year-old law that names a mechanism every debasement produces. T1: in 1560 THOMAS GRESHAM, an English merchant and royal financial advisor, wrote a letter to the newly-crowned Queen Elizabeth I explaining why England's coinage was in trouble. His formulation, later shortened to the maxim we now know: 'BAD MONEY DRIVES OUT GOOD.' T2: what the law actually says. When TWO COINS with the SAME FACE VALUE but DIFFERENT INTRINSIC VALUE (metal content) circulate together by law, people SPEND the debased coin and HOARD the good one. The market fills with bad coin; the good coin disappears from circulation. T3: HOW IT WORKS mechanically. Suppose a full-silver shilling and a half-silver shilling are both legal tender at one shilling. A rational person paying for bread hands over the half-silver coin (worth less) and keeps the full-silver coin (worth more). Merchants receive only half-silver coins. Full-silver coins get melted for their metal value or exported to countries where they trade at true weight. Within months, only debased coins circulate at home. T4: the LAW HAD OLDER OBSERVERS. NICHOLAS COPERNICUS (astronomer, but also a monetary theorist for the Prussian estates) wrote in 1526 in Monetae cudendae ratio that 'when new, better coin is introduced, the old is not withdrawn but hoarded, and this creates unrest.' NICOLE ORESME, a 14th-century French bishop and monetary thinker, had written the same insight in De Moneta (c. 1360) -- 200 years before Gresham. The law was renamed for Gresham in the 19th century by the economist Henry Dunning Macleod, who found Gresham's letter in the archives. T5: WHERE THE LAW APPLIES TODAY. The classic modern case: US SILVER COINS pre-1965. When the US Coinage Act of 1965 removed silver from dimes and quarters, Americans within a few years pulled all the pre-1965 silver coins out of pocket-change circulation and hoarded them -- the copper-nickel coins had 'driven them out.' The same mechanism: even the informal user-community will separate sound money from debased once the discrepancy is large enough.

name: The Crime of '73 and Bryan's Cross of Gold (1873-1896)

scope: The 19th-century American money debate that produced one of the most famous political speeches ever given. T1: in 1873 the US COINAGE ACT quietly ended the free coinage of silver, effectively moving the United States to a pure gold standard. Silver interests -- mining states, agricultural debtors, populist reformers -- soon called this the CRIME OF '73, alleging (probably wrongly, per most historians) that it was a conspiracy of Eastern bankers to enrich creditors at farmers' expense. T2: the 1873 act mattered because a stronger dollar made DEBTS HARDER TO REPAY. Farmers who had borrowed to buy land and equipment during the Civil War greenback era found that their crops sold for fewer dollars while their debts stayed nominally the same. Falling prices (deflation) transferred wealth from debtors to creditors. T3: the POLITICAL RESPONSE. By the 1890s the FREE SILVER movement was a full political force, demanding that the US resume unlimited coinage of silver at the traditional 16-to-1 ratio to gold (which would have effectively re-monetized silver as a second money and inflated the currency to help debtors). The Democratic Party split -- 'Gold Democrats' backing Cleveland; 'Silver Democrats' rising with the young Nebraska congressman WILLIAM JENNINGS BRYAN. T4: THE CROSS OF GOLD SPEECH. On July 8 1896 at the Democratic National Convention in Chicago, Bryan, aged 36, closed his address with lines that would be quoted for a century: 'You shall not press down upon the brow of labor this crown of thorns; you shall not crucify mankind upon a CROSS OF GOLD.' The delegates carried him around the hall on their shoulders. He won the nomination that afternoon. T5: WHAT HAPPENED NEXT and what it teaches. Bryan lost the general election to Republican WILLIAM McKINLEY in November 1896. New gold discoveries in the Klondike (1896), South Africa's Witwatersrand, and Colorado inflated the gold money supply organically over the next decade -- prices rose, debtors were relieved, and the silver question quietly died. name: WW1 and the collapse of the classical gold standard
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: How the war that no one wanted was funded by breaking the money that had prevented it. T1: in the FIRST WEEK OF AUGUST 1914, as the great powers mobilized for war, EACH BELLIGERENT SUSPENDED GOLD CONVERTIBILITY -- meaning their citizens and foreign holders of their currency could no longer redeem paper money for gold. Germany suspended August 4; Britain in effect August 6 (though technically maintaining formal gold-standard status); France, Russia, Austria-Hungary all followed within the same week. T2: WHY. Fighting a modern industrial war costs vast sums per day. Under gold discipline, governments could raise money only by TAXING (unpopular, slow) or BORROWING (limited by lender willingness). Off the gold standard, they could PRINT paper money to pay for shells, ships, and soldiers -- and defer the reckoning until after victory. T3: WHAT PRINTING PRODUCED. Every belligerent's money supply exploded during the war. Germany's outstanding paper notes grew about 12x from 1914 to 1918. Britain's price level roughly doubled. France's roughly tripled. Russia's currency (the ruble) collapsed entirely during the 1917 revolution. Only the United States, entering the war late (April 1917) and less committed to spending, kept relative monetary discipline. T4: THE AUSTRIAN COUNTERFACTUAL that makes this rung load-bearing. Under the FULL classical gold standard, WW1 could not have been fought for four years. Governments would have run out of GOLD to borrow within months and would have been forced to a negotiated settlement. The four years of industrial-scale slaughter (~17 million dead) was ECONOMICALLY POSSIBLE only because paper-money printing had been unleashed. Ludwig von Mises made this argument explicitly in his 1919 book Nation, State, and Economy. T5: THE POSTWAR REPAIR ATTEMPTS. From 1919 through 1925 nations tried to return to gold. Britain returned in 1925 at the PREWAR PARITY (Churchill as Chancellor, on advice from Bank of England officials -- a decision Keynes famously attacked in 'The Economic Consequences of Mr. Churchill'), which forced painful deflation. The Genoa Conference of 1922 proposed a GOLD-EXCHANGE STANDARD (weaker version: only central banks hold gold; commercial reserves are foreign currencies redeemable for gold). This interwar system was already collapsing by 1931 when Britain permanently abandoned gold, and it died fully with WW2. The MOVE the ladder teaches: SOUND MONEY IS A CONSTRAINT ON GOVERNMENT POWER; states that want to fight big wars ALWAYS want to be freed from that constraint; the 20th century's political catastrophes and its monetary catastrophes are the SAME EVENT.

name: Weimar hyperinflation (1921-1923): the wheelbarrow scenes

scope: The most vivid hyperinflation in modern memory, and the one that made 'wheelbarrow of cash' the world's mental image for currency collapse. T1: after WW1, Germany's REICHSBANK -- freed from gold discipline in August 1914 and burdened with Versailles reparations -- kept printing PAPERMARK. Through 1921 and early 1922 the mark's decline was steep but not yet catastrophic; from mid-1922 the collapse accelerated exponentially. T2: THE SPECIFIC NUMBERS. In January 1922 one US dollar bought about 190 marks. By January 1923, it bought about 18,000 marks. By July 1923, 353,000. By August, 4.6 million. By October, 25 BILLION. The peak monthly rate came in October 1923: about 29,500 PERCENT inflation IN ONE MONTH -- prices roughly doubling every two days. T3: THE SCENES that got recorded in photographs and memoirs. Workers paid TWICE A DAY and running to shops before prices doubled between morning and afternoon shifts. Wheelbarrows of banknotes carried to buy a single loaf of bread. Children building block towers out of bundled 100,000-mark notes because paper had less use-value than firewood. A woman leaving a shopping basket unguarded had the basket stolen -- the money inside was thrown on the sidewalk. Cafes announced prices at the START of coffee and again when the bill arrived (higher). T4: THE STOP. In November 1923, Finance Minister HJALMAR SCHACHT introduced the RENTENMARK, backed nominally by a mortgage on German industrial and agricultural land. The exchange rate at conversion: ONE RENTENMARK equaled ONE TRILLION (1,000,000,000,000) PAPERMARK. Confidence returned within weeks. Prices stabilized. The whole hyperinflation had run its course in about 27 MONTHS. T5: WHAT WAS DESTROYED. The middle class -- German professionals and small savers who had kept their savings in bonds and cash -- was WIPED OUT financially. The urban working class, whose weekly wages could be spent immediately, was less devastated than the retired doctor with a lifetime of savings in mark-denominated bonds. Rural farmers with real assets did comparatively well. This ASYMMETRIC DESTRUCTION -- Cantillon in real time -- helped destroy the political center of the Weimar Republic and prepared the ground for what came ten years later. The Austrian point: SEEN was 'money still being paid'; UNSEEN was the lifetime savings of an entire generation of German savers evaporating in 27 months.

name: Bretton Woods (1944): the dollar-gold anchor

scope: The 1944 conference that set the postwar monetary order -- and how a Soviet asset helped design it. Foreign central banks (but not private citizens or foreign private holders) could redeem dollars for gold at that rate. The US would hold the world's largest gold reserve as the anchor. Two new institutions -- the INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND (IMF) to manage exchange-rate stability, and the WORLD BANK (formally the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development) to fund postwar reconstruction -- were created. T3: THE KEYNES vs WHITE DEBATE. Britain's chief delegate JOHN MAYNARD KEYNES proposed the BANCOR: a supranational reserve currency issued by a global 'International Clearing Union', with the pound and dollar as equal contributors. The US chief delegate HARRY DEXTER WHITE proposed the dollar-anchor system that was adopted. Britain, financially destroyed by the war and dependent on US loans, had no leverage; the US design won. name: De Gaulle's gold drain and the London Gold Pool (1965-1968)
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The specific European action that revealed the Bretton Woods system was already broken. T1: by the mid-1960s the US was RUNNING DEFICITS to fund the Vietnam War and Lyndon Johnson's Great Society programs; the dollar was becoming increasingly OVERVALUED at the $35/oz Bretton Woods peg. Foreign central banks, holding growing dollar reserves, began wondering whether the US could actually deliver gold if asked. T2: FRANCE ASKED. In February 1965, at a press conference, French President CHARLES DE GAULLE denounced the 'exorbitant privilege' the dollar gave the United States -- the ability to run deficits paid in its own printed currency -- and announced France would systematically convert its dollar reserves to gold at the official $35 peg. T3: THE PHRASE 'EXORBITANT PRIVILEGE.' It was coined by de Gaulle's finance minister VALERY GISCARD D'ESTAING (later President of France 1974-81), not by de Gaulle himself, though it is popularly associated with de Gaulle's 1965 speech. The phrase captures the deep asymmetry: the US could import goods and pay in newly-printed dollars; those dollars accumulated in foreign banks; the world was effectively lending the US real goods in exchange for paper claims. T4: FRANCE'S ACTUAL GOLD SHIPMENTS 1965-71. France converted about $150 million of dollar reserves to gold in 1965 alone; over the next several years French warships literally sailed to New York to bring gold home from the Federal Reserve Bank of New York's vault (the Manhattan bedrock vault at 33 Liberty Street holding foreign central-bank gold). Other central banks followed France's lead more quietly. T5: THE LONDON GOLD POOL COLLAPSE, March 1968. To hold the $35 peg against rising private gold demand, EIGHT Western central banks (USA, UK, France, Germany, Italy, Belgium, Netherlands, Switzerland) had pooled their gold reserves in 1961 as a defensive mechanism, selling into any private-market run to hold the price. France had already withdrawn from the pool in June 1967. By March 1968 the remaining pool members had lost so much gold defending the peg that they gave up -- the pool was dissolved March 17 1968 and a TWO-TIER MARKET emerged: $35 for central-bank transactions, market-determined price for private buyers. This was Bretton Woods' effective death; the Nixon shock three years later was the formal funeral. RECOGNITION MOVE: SEEN a stable $35 gold-dollar peg backed by US reserves; UNSEEN the arithmetic that once dollar-issuance outran gold reserves, the peg was ARITHMETICALLY IMPOSSIBLE and would break the moment any large holder tested it. name: Zimbabwe 2007-2009: the $100 trillion note
strand: Gold + fiat history: what makes Bitcoin necessary
scope: The 21st-century case that produced the highest-denomination banknote ever printed. T1: from 2000, ZIMBABWE'S President ROBERT MUGABE ordered the SEIZURE of white-owned commercial farms as part of a 'land reform' program. The farms -- which had provided most of Zimbabwe's grain and export earnings -- collapsed in production. Government tax revenue collapsed with them. To pay the army and civil service, the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe began PRINTING money on an accelerating scale. T2: THE INFLATION CURVE. By 2007, monthly inflation was in the thousands of percent. By mid-2008, tens of thousands. In NOVEMBER 2008, monthly inflation reached an official peak of 79.6 BILLION PERCENT -- prices doubling roughly every 24 HOURS. This is the second-highest hyperinflation in human history (after Hungary's July 1946 pengo, at 41.9 quadrillion percent monthly). T3: THE $100 TRILLION NOTE. In JANUARY 2009 the Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issued a 100,000,000,000,000-Zimbabwe-dollar banknote -- the HIGHEST DENOMINATION BANKNOTE EVER ISSUED by any government in monetary history. When issued, it bought roughly three eggs. T4: THE SCENES. Zimbabweans were paid in the morning and ran to spend before afternoon-shift wages arrived at higher prices. Shopkeepers rewrote prices multiple times a day. Bread lines formed. Fuel stations closed. Formal economy collapsed and USD-cash barter emerged spontaneously; by 2009 the country ABANDONED the Zimbabwe dollar entirely and began using foreign currencies (US dollar, South African rand, Botswana pula) as everyday money. The Zimbabwe dollar was formally demonetized in June 2015; the government paid holders 175 QUADRILLION Zimbabwe dollars for one US dollar. T5: THE COLLECTOR MARKET AND WHAT IT TEACHES. Zimbabwe's $100 trillion notes are now sold worldwide as SOUVENIRS for $2-15 USD each -- a physical, cheap, permanent reminder to any Western student of what fiat-currency collapse looks like. The mechanism was TEXTBOOK Austrian: fiscal deficit (land-seizure collapse of the tax base) plus central-bank money-printing to close the deficit produced Cantillon-effect asymmetric destruction of savers, then hyperinflation, then abandonment. The RECOGNITION MOVE: modern hyperinflations are NOT relics of the 1920s -- they happen NOW, in Africa, in Latin America, in the modern world, whenever the same mechanism runs. This is not history; this is a live monetary experiment students can watch on YouTube today.

name: Every fiat currency dies: the 5,000-year pattern

Confederate States dollar (1861-1865, collapsed with the Confederacy). German papermark (1914-1923, hyperinflated in 9 years). Hungarian pengo (1927-1946, world-record hyperinflation). Argentine peso cycles (multiple collapses: 1989, 2001, 2018, 2023). Yugoslav dinar (1992-94 hyperinflation). Zimbabwean dollar (2000-2009 hyperinflation, formally demonetized 2015). Venezuelan bolivar (2016-present hyperinflation). Lebanese pound (2019-present, -98%). T3: THE CURRENT FIAT CURRENCIES all began after the 1971 Nixon shock's abandonment of gold anchoring. British pound sterling, 1,300 years old? -- has lost 99.5% of purchasing power since 1750; the physical coin composition changed from silver to nickel; the modern paper pound is a completely different monetary regime from the medieval silver penny. Swiss franc, 'the world's most stable currency'? -- lost gold backing 2000; has depreciated substantially against gold ever since. Japanese yen? -- surviving in nominal form but at massive real-value loss (1971 yen to 2024 yen: substantial depreciation against gold). No fiat is exempt. The pattern is not accident -- it flows from the STRUCTURAL INCENTIVE facing any monetary authority: politicians promise citizens more than tax revenue supports, monetary authorities close the gap by printing, printing debases the currency, savers absorb the loss, the pattern accumulates until confidence breaks. The pattern has repeated for 5,000 years across every civilization that tried unbacked paper money. This is the empirical case for SOUND MONEY as an engineering problem, not a political one -- the case that culminated in SATOSHI NAKAMOTO'S 2008 Bitcoin white paper, which attempted to solve the political-money problem with cryptography and consensus rather than trust. Whether Bitcoin succeeds is a live question; that fiat has ALWAYS failed is a historical fact.
